en: The Sutra on the Inconceivable Realm of the Buddhas Spoken by Mañjuśrī,
Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Tang Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of one thousand bhikṣus and ten thousand bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, there were various devaputras of the desire realm, various devaputras of the form realm, and the devaputras of the Pure Abodes, together with their retinues numbering in the hundreds of thousands, surrounding him on all sides, making offerings and paying respect as they listened to the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Young man!
You possess eloquence and are well able to expound and elaborate upon it."
"You should now proclaim the sublime Dharma for the great assembly of bodhisattvas.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Buddha, what Dharma should you now have me expound?
The Buddha said, "O youth!"
“You should now explain the realm of all Buddhas.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said,
“World-Honored One!”

The realm of the Buddhas is not the realm of the eye, nor the realm of form; it is not the realm of the ear, nor the realm of sound; it is not the realm of the nose, nor the realm of fragrance; it is not the realm of the tongue, nor the realm of flavor; it is not the realm of the body, nor the realm of touch; it is not the realm of the mind, nor the realm of phenomena. Being devoid of such differentiated realms, this is what is called the realm of all Buddhas.
“World-Honored One!
If good sons and good daughters wish to enter the realm of the Buddha, they must take ‘non-entry’ as their skillful means in order to be able to awaken to and enter it.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Within what kind of realm does the Tathāgata attain bodhi?”
The Buddha said,
"Young man!
I attained bodhi within the realm of emptiness, because all views are equal."
One attains bodhi through the realm of signlessness, because all signs are equal;
one attains bodhi through the realm of wishlessness, because the three realms are equal;
one attains bodhi through the realm of non-action, because all conditioned phenomena are equal.
“O Youth!
I have attained bodhi in the realm that is unborn, unarisen, and unconditioned, because all conditioned phenomena are equal.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the sphere of the unconditioned?
The Buddha said:
“O youth! The unconditioned is not within the sphere of discursive thought.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
That which is not within the realm of discursive thought is the realm of the Buddha. Why is this so?
Within the realm that transcends discursive thought, there are no words.
Because there are no words, there is nothing to be explained or discoursed upon.
Because there is nothing to be explained or discoursed upon, all verbal discourse is cut off.
"That which transcends all discursive speech is the realm of the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: "O Youth!"
“Where should one seek the realm of all Buddhas?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva replied,
“World-Honored One!”
The realm of all Buddhas should be sought within the afflictions of all sentient beings.
Why is this? Because if one correctly understands the afflictions of sentient beings, that itself is the realm of all Buddhas.
"This correct understanding of the afflictions of sentient beings is the realm of the Buddhas; it is not a domain traversed by any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Young man!"
“If the realm of the Buddhas is sought right within the afflictions of all sentient beings,
does that realm of the Buddhas have coming or going? Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva replied, “No.”
“World-Honored One!
The realm of all Buddhas is without coming and without going.
The Buddha said:
“O youth, if the realm of all Buddhas is neither coming nor going, why do you say that the thorough understanding of the afflictions of sentient beings is itself the realm of all Buddhas?”
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
"World-Honored One!
Just as the realm of the Buddhas has neither coming nor going, so too is the intrinsic nature of all afflictions likewise without coming or going."
The Buddha said:
"Young man! What is the intrinsic nature of these afflictions?"
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
The intrinsic nature of the Buddha’s realm is itself the intrinsic nature of all afflictions.”
World-Honored One!
If the intrinsic nature of the Buddha’s realm were different from the intrinsic nature of the various afflictions, the Tathāgata would not be the perfectly awakened one of equality.
Because they are not different, he has attained equal and perfect awakening regarding all phenomena; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī,
saying: "Young man,
are you able to fully understand the equal Dharma in which the Tathāgata abides?"
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
I have already understood.”
The Buddha said:
"Young man! What is the dharmic equality in which the Tathāgata dwells?"
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
The very places where all ordinary beings give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion are the dharmas of equality in which the Tathāgata dwells.”
The Buddha said: "Young man,
how is it that the very basis upon which all ordinary beings give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion is the state of equality in which the Tathāgata dwells?"
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!

All ordinary beings give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion within the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; therefore, the very place where all ordinary beings give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion is precisely the state of equality in which the Tathāgata dwells.”
The Buddha said:
“O youth! How could emptiness be a dharma that exists, such that one speaks of greed, hatred, and delusion within it?”
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One, emptiness exists; therefore, greed, hatred, and delusion also exist.
The Buddha said:
“Young man!
How can emptiness exist?
And how can greed, hatred, and delusion exist?”
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
Emptiness exists because of verbal expression; greed, hatred, and delusion also exist because of verbal expression.”
As the Buddha said:
"O Bhikṣus! There is that which is unborn, unarisen, unconditioned, and uncreated; it is not a dharma of conditioned formations."
This is without birth, without arising, without activity, and unconditioned; it is not a phenomenon of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), yet it is not non-existent.
If it were non-existent, then regarding the phenomena of conditioned formations—birth, arising, and activity—there would be no transcendence.
"It is because [emptiness] exists that one speaks of transcendence.
This is also the case here: if emptiness did not exist, there would be no transcendence from greed, hatred, and delusion.
Because emptiness exists, it is said that one is free from the various afflictions such as greed.
The Buddha said:
"Young man! So it is, so it is;
it is just as you have said."
"All afflictions, such as greed, hatred, and delusion, do not fail to abide within emptiness.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If a practitioner seeks emptiness while remaining detached from greed, hatred, and the like, one should know that this person has not yet skillfully practiced; they cannot be called a true practitioner.
"Why is this? It is because all afflictions, such as greed, hatred, and delusion, are themselves emptiness.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Young man!
Have you already emerged from greed, hatred, and delusion, or have you not yet emerged from them?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva replied:
“World-Honored One!

The nature of greed, hatred, and delusion is itself equality; I always abide in such equality. Therefore, regarding greed, hatred, and delusion, I have neither departed from them nor am I not yet departed.”
"Bhagavān!
If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who perceive themselves as being free from greed, hatred, and delusion, yet perceive others as having greed, hatred, and delusion, these constitute two views."
What are the two views?
They are the view of annihilationism and the view of eternalism. Why is this so?
If one perceives one's own body as being free from greed, hatred, and delusion, this is the view of annihilationism;
if one perceives the bodies of others as possessing greed, hatred, and delusion, this is the view of eternalism.
World-Honored One!
"Such a person does not abide in the correct state.
One who abides correctly should not regard themselves as superior or consider others as inferior.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
“O youth! If it is thus, abiding in what place is called ‘right abiding’?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva replied:
“World-Honored One!
As for one who dwells correctly, there is nothing upon which they dwell; dwelling in non-dwelling—this alone is called ‘dwelling correctly.
The Buddha said:
“O Youth! Is it not the case that abiding in the right path constitutes right dwelling?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva replied:
“World-Honored One!
If one dwells in the path of right practice, then one dwells in the conditioned.
If one dwells in the conditioned, then one does not dwell in the equality of the dharma-nature.”
"Why is this? Because conditioned phenomena possess arising and ceasing.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
“O youth! Is the unconditioned a numerical phenomenon?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva replied:
“World-Honored One!
The unconditioned is not a numerical phenomenon.
World-Honored One!”
"If unconditioned phenomena were to fall within the realm of enumeration, they would be conditioned, not unconditioned.
The Buddha said,
"Young man!"
“Do all noble ones who have attained the unconditioned dharma not possess numbers?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said,
“World-Honored One!”
"It is not that the noble ones realize numerical phenomena, for they have already attained liberation from all numerical phenomena.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Young man!"
"Do you accomplish the noble dharmas, or do you accomplish the non-noble dharmas?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"I neither accomplish noble dharmas nor do I accomplish non-noble dharmas.
World-Honored One, suppose there were a conjured person; would they accomplish noble dharmas or would they accomplish non-noble dharmas?"
The Buddha said: "Young man!
A person who is an emanation cannot be said to have accomplished the noble dharmas, nor can they be said to have accomplished the non-noble dharmas."
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
"World-Honored One,
has the Buddha not indeed taught that all dharmas are like illusions and transformations?"
The Buddha said, “It is so.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
All dharmas are like the appearance of illusions and transformations; I, too, am thus. How can it be said that I accomplish noble dharmas or accomplish non-noble dharmas?”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Young man, if it is thus, what have you attained?”
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
I have attained the realm of the Tathāgata’s equality, which is without intrinsic nature.”
The Buddha said,
"Young man!
Have you attained the realm of a Buddha?"
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
"If the World-Honored One had anything to be attained within the realm of the Buddhas, I too would have attained the realms of all Buddhas."
At that time, the Elder Subhūti asked the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
“O Mahāsattva!
Does the Tathāgata not attain the realm of a Buddha?”
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
"Virtuous One!
Have you attained the realm of a śrāvaka?"
Subhūti said: "O Great Being!
The noble mind is liberated and possesses no objective sphere; therefore, I now have no objective sphere to be found."
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
"Virtuous One!
The Buddha is also like this; his mind is liberated and possesses no objective realm. How, then, can it be said that there is anything to be attained?"
Subhūti said: "O Mahāsattva!
As you now preach the Dharma, will you not protect the minds of those who are beginners?"
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
"Virtuous One!
I now question you; answer as you see fit."

Suppose there were a skilled physician who wished to treat a person's illness; for the sake of protecting that patient's mind, he did not provide the bitter, sour, salty, or pungent medicines appropriate for the disease—could he cause that person's illness to be cured and reach a state of peace and well-being?
He replied, “No. Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
"Venerable One! It is just the same in this case.

If a Dharma teacher, for the sake of protecting the minds of beginners, conceals the most profound teachings and does not expound them, but instead preaches only coarse and superficial meanings according to their own inclinations, it is impossible that such a teacher can enable students to emerge from the suffering of birth and death and reach the bliss of Nirvana."
When this Dharma was being taught, there were five hundred bhikṣus in the assembly whose outflows were forever exhausted and whose minds attained liberation.
Eight hundred devaputras, having distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Furthermore, seven hundred devaputras, hearing his eloquence, conceived deep faith and joy, and all resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Great Being!
Do you also give rise to faith and understanding in the Śrāvaka Vehicle, and do you also deliver sentient beings by means of this vehicle?"
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
"Virtuous One!
I give rise to faith and understanding in all vehicles."
“Venerable Sir!
I have faith and understanding in the Śrāvaka-yāna, I also have faith and understanding in the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, and I also have faith and understanding in the Samyaksaṃbuddha-yāna. Subhūti said:
“Great Being! Are you a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, or a samyaksaṃbuddha?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva replied:
“Virtuous One!
Although I am a śrāvaka, I have not heard [the Dharma] from another;
although I am a pratyekabuddha, I do not abandon great compassion and fearlessness.”
"Although you have already attained perfect enlightenment, you never cease from all that ought to be done.
Subhūti asked again: "O Great Being!"
"How can you be a śrāvaka?
He replied, "I constantly preach the Dharma never heard before to all sentient beings; for this reason, I am a śrāvaka."
He asked again,
"In what way are you a pratyekabuddha?
He replied:
"I am able to understand that all phenomena arise from conditions; therefore, I am a pratyekabuddha.
He asked again:
"In what way are you a samyaksaṃbuddha?"
He replied:
"I am constantly and eternally awakened to the fact that the essential nature and characteristics of all phenomena are equal; for this reason, I am a Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, Subhūti asked again:
“O Mahāsattva!
In which stage do you definitively abide?
Do you abide in the stage of a śrāvaka?”
"Does he abide in the stage of a pratyekabuddha,
or does he abide in the stage of a buddha?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva replied:
“Venerable One!
You should know that I am firmly established in all the stages. Subhūti said:
“O Mahāsattva!
Can you also definitively abide in the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana)?
He replied:
"It is so. Why is this? Because the nature of all dharmas and all sentient beings is itself the definitive state of correctness."
"I always abide in this state of right position; therefore, I say that I am definitively established in the stage of an ordinary person.
Subhūti asked again:

"If all dharmas and all sentient beings are themselves this definitive state of right position, how can one establish the distinctions between the various stages, saying, 'This is the stage of an ordinary person,' 'This is the stage of a śrāvaka,' 'This is the stage of a pratyekabuddha,' and 'This is the stage of a Buddha'?"
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
"Virtuous One!

For example, in the world, by means of verbal designation, one establishes the ten directions within empty space, saying: 'This is the east,' 'This is the south,' and so on, up to 'This is the zenith' and 'This is the nadir.'"
Although space is without differentiation, yet the various directions possess such and such diverse distinctions. This is likewise so:

within the definitive state of absolute reality, the Tathāgata, by means of skillful expedients, establishes the various stages, declaring: "This is the stage of ordinary beings; this is the stage of śrāvakas; this is the stage of pratyekabuddhas; this is the stage of bodhisattvas; and this is the stage of buddhas."
"Although the true position (bhūmi) is without differentiation, there are nonetheless distinctions among the various stages.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"O Mahāsattva!"
"Have you already entered the stage of certainty?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva replied,
"Virtuous One!"
"Although I have already entered, I have likewise not entered.
Subhūti said, "O Mahāsattva!"
"What is it to have already entered yet not to enter?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva replied,
"Virtuous One!
You should know that this is the skillful wisdom of a bodhisattva.
I shall now speak a parable for you, for those who possess intelligence gain understanding through parables.
"Venerable Sir!

Suppose there were a master archer whose skill was preeminent, who had an only son whom he cherished with particular affection, and who moreover had a most bitter enemy whom he would not wish to hear mentioned nor even look upon."
Once, while his son was wandering abroad, he stood by the side of the road at a great distance.
Seeing him from afar, the father mistook him for an enemy; seizing his bow and arrow, he drew the string and shot.
Once the arrow had been released, he realized it was his son; being skillful and agile, he ran swiftly to pursue the arrow and recovered it before it could reach its mark.
Here, the master archer is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva; the only son is a metaphor for sentient beings; and the enemy is a metaphor for the afflictions (*kleśa*).
As for the term "arrow," it is a metaphor for noble wisdom.

Venerable sir, you should know that because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates all phenomena through the Prajñāpāramitā, and by virtue of the skillful means of great compassion regarding the station of non-arising, he does not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and thus does not abide in the stages of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha; rather, he vows to transform and deliver all sentient beings until they reach the stage of Buddhahood.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Great Being! What kind of bodhisattva is able to practice this conduct?"
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
"Virtuous One!
If a bodhisattva manifests conduct within the world yet is not defiled by worldly dharmas;
They manifest in accordance with the world, yet they do not give rise to views regarding any phenomena;
although they exert diligent effort to sever the afflictions of all sentient beings, they enter the dharma-realm without perceiving any sign of exhaustion;
although they do not abide in the conditioned, they likewise do not attain the unconditioned.
Though dwelling in birth and death, they are like those strolling through a garden;
because their original vows are not yet fulfilled, they do not seek the swift realization of unsurpassed nirvana;
though they deeply understand non-self, they constantly transform sentient beings.
Although they contemplate that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is like empty space, they diligently cultivate merit and purify the Buddha-lands;
although they enter the Dharma-realm and perceive the equality of all phenomena, they do not abandon diligence in order to adorn the Buddha’s actions of body, speech, and mind.
"If Bodhisattvas possess such conduct as this, they are indeed able to practice.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"O Mahāsattva!"
"What you have now spoken regarding the conduct of these bodhisattvas is not something that can be believed or accepted by those in the world.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
"Virtuous One!..."

"I now wish to cause all sentient beings to transcend the world forever; therefore, I shall explain the practice of transcending the world through which Bodhisattvas thoroughly understand worldly phenomena.
Subhūti said, "O Great Being!"
"What are the worldly dharmas?
What is called renunciation?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva replied:
"Venerable Sir!
As for worldly phenomena, they are what are called the five aggregates.
What are these five?"
They are the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.

These aggregates are such that form is like a mass of foam, feeling is like a bubble on the water, perception is like a mirage, formations are like a plantain tree, and consciousness is like a magical illusion. Therefore, herein there is no world, nor are there these aggregates, nor such verbal designations and names.
If one attains this understanding, the mind will not be distracted.
If the mind is not distracted, it will not be defiled by worldly dharmas.
If it is not defiled by worldly dharmas, this is precisely the transcendence of worldly dharmas.
"Furthermore, Venerable Sir!
The phenomena of the five aggregates are by nature fundamentally empty.

That which is empty by nature is non-dual; that which is non-dual is devoid of self and what belongs to a self. Being devoid of self and what belongs to a self, there is nothing to be grasped or attached to. This absence of grasping and attachment is precisely the transcendence of worldly dharmas."
"Furthermore, Venerable Sir, as for the phenomena of the five aggregates, they exist by way of causes and conditions.

Because they exist by way of causes and conditions, they lack inherent power; lacking power, they have no master; having no master, there is neither self nor what belongs to a self; having neither self nor what belongs to a self, there is no grasping or appropriation; having no grasping or appropriation, there is no contention; and having no contention, there is no dispute. This absence of dispute is the Dharma of the śramaṇa. The Dharma of the śramaṇa is to know all phenomena to be like echoes in the sky. To be able to fully comprehend that all phenomena are like echoes in the sky is precisely the Dharma of transcendence from the world."
"Furthermore, Venerable Sir!
These five aggregates are identical to the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The dharma-realm is itself no realm; within that which is not a realm, there is no eye-realm, no form-realm, and no eye-consciousness-realm."
There is no ear element, no sound element, and no ear-consciousness element;
there is no nose element, no odor element, and no nose-consciousness element;
there is no tongue element, no taste element, and no tongue-consciousness element.
There is no body-element, no touch-element, and no body-consciousness-element;
there is no mind-element, no phenomena-element, and no mind-consciousness-element.
Within this, there is also no earth-element, water-element, fire-element, wind-element, space-element, or consciousness-element.
Furthermore, there is no realm of desire, realm of form, or realm of formlessness;
nor is there a conditioned realm or an unconditioned realm.
Such things as self, person, sentient being, and life-span—none of these exist at all, and they are definitively unattainable.
"If one can enter this profound meaning of equality and accord with that which has no entry, this is precisely the transcendence of worldly dharmas.
When this teaching was spoken, two hundred bhikṣus in the assembly forever exhausted all outflows, and their minds attained liberation.
Each of them removed the upper garment they were wearing and offered it to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, saying these words:
"If there are sentient beings who hear this profound and wondrous Dharma, they should give rise to faith and accept it."
"If one does not give rise to faith, yet desires to seek realization, it can never be attained.
At that time, the Elder Subhūti addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"What have you attained? By what do you realize [the truth]?"
The bhikṣus said:
"Venerable One!
Neither attaining nor realizing—this is the dharma of a śramaṇa."
Why is this so? If there is anything attained, the mind becomes agitated and distracted.
If there is anything realized, one becomes self-conceited and arrogant.
"To be agitated and conceited is to fall into the works of Māra.
If anyone says of themselves, 'I have attained' or 'I have realized,' you should know that such a person is one of overweening pride.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“Monks! Do you clearly understand the meaning of ‘overweening pride’?
The monks replied:
“World-Honored One!
According to my understanding, if someone says, ‘I am able to know suffering,’ they do not know the characteristic of suffering;
and if they say, ‘I know it, I am able to abandon the origin, realize cessation, and cultivate the path,’ they do not know the characteristics of the origin, cessation, and the path.”
Even to say, "I am able to cultivate the Path," one should know that this person is one of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Why is this? Because the characteristic of suffering (*duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*) is itself the characteristic of non-arising (*anutpāda-lakṣaṇa*).
The characteristics of origination, cessation, and the path are themselves the characteristic of non-arising.
That which is the characteristic of non-arising is the absence of characteristics and the characteristic of equality.

These noble ones attain the characteristic of liberation regarding all phenomena; within this, no such characteristics as "knowing suffering," "abandoning origination," "realizing cessation," or "cultivating the path" can be found.

If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing such meanings as the equality of all dharmas, give rise to fear and trepidation, you should know that they are those possessed of overweening pride (adhimāna).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed them, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, O bhikṣus!"
"It is as you have said; it is so, it is so, Subhūti!
You should know that these bhikṣus have already, in the past, at the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, heard such a profound Dharma from the youth Mañjuśrī."
Because they have heard the Dharma, they quickly attained supernormal powers; now hearing it again, they accord with it and do not oppose it. Subhūti!
If there are others who, within my Dharma, hear this meaning and give rise to faith and understanding, they shall all see Maitreya Buddha in a future life.
Those who have not yet resolved to attain the Great Vehicle will all achieve liberation within the three assemblies.
Those who have already resolved to attain the Great Vehicle will all abide in the stage of endurance (*kṣānti*).
At that time, the Devaputra Suvikrānta addressed Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Mahāsattva!
You constantly preach the Dharma for the sake of the multitudes here within this Jambudvīpa."

Now, there are devaputras in the Tuṣita Heaven who, having encountered immeasurable Buddhas in the past, made offerings and showed them respect, planting various roots of goodness; yet, because they have been born in the heavens and become attached to sensory realms, they are unable to come to this Dharma assembly to listen and receive the teaching.
In the past they planted roots of goodness, yet now they are on the verge of losing them; if they receive your guidance and instruction, they will surely grow further.
We pray that you, Great Being, will temporarily visit the celestial palaces to extensively proclaim the essentials of the Dharma for those devas.

At that time, by means of his supernatural powers, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī suddenly manifested a Tuṣita Heaven palace right there, complete with every requisite detail. He caused the Son of Heaven, Sudharmajaya, and all the gods and humans in this assembly to believe they were actually in that celestial realm.
He beheld there various adornments: groves and gardens with ponds, rows of fruit trees, palaces and towers where the rafters and eaves met;
embroidered pillars supporting the beams, carved windows set between the doors, and a profusion of clustered capitals and layered brackets distributed in a magnificent array.

Heaped up treasures to form terraces, adorned with exquisite and intricate patterns; these terraces were at their smallest still seven stories high, or eight, nine, and even as many as twenty stories tall.

Upon each terrace, at every level, there were numerous celestial maidens of youthful age and exquisite beauty; their hands and feet were soft and supple, their foreheads broad and their eyebrows long, and their faces were pure and serene.
Like a golden lattice net, he was constantly radiant; like a lotus flower, he was free from all dust and defilement.
When speaking, he smiled; in his advancing, retreating, turning, and circling, every movement accorded with propriety—beauteous yet governed by rule.
It was like the full moon, which all people delight in beholding.

There were lutes, harps, zithers, and lyres; flutes, pipes, bells, and drums; some singing and others whistling, their melodies harmonizing together. Rows of exquisite dancers moved in formation, dancing together across the courtyard; all such things were clearly visible before one's eyes.

At that time, the Devaputra Subhavyūha, having witnessed the splendor of his own palace and the joyful amusements of his retinue, felt a sense of wonder and doubt, and addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"How marvelous!"
"O Great Being!
How did you cause me and this great assembly to arrive here in the space of a single moment?
At that time, the Elder Subhūti spoke to the Devaputra Suvikrānta:
“O Son of Heaven!

At first, I also thought that I had gone together with the great assembly to the Tuṣita Heaven; now I know that from the very beginning there was no movement, and I never actually went to that celestial realm.”
"All that which has been seen is merely a manifestation of the samādhi and supernatural powers of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.
At that time, the Devaputra Suśobhana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī is truly most rare, for by means of the inconceivable power of his samādhi and supernormal faculties, he has caused this assembly to reach the Tuṣita Heaven without moving from their original place.
The Buddha said, “Devaputra, you know only a small portion of the power of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta’s supernormal transformations; that which I know is immeasurable.”
"O Son of Heaven!

By the supernatural power of Mañjuśrī, even if there were as many Buddha-lands as the sands of the Ganges River, each adorned with various distinct splendors, he could cause them all to be clearly seen within a single Buddha-land."
Furthermore, he can gather as many Buddha-lands as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River into a single place, like a bundle of silk, and cast them upward without finding it difficult to do so.

Furthermore, he places all the great oceans within as many Buddha-lands as there are sands in the Ganges into a single pore, yet causes the sentient beings therein to neither perceive nor know it, and to remain untouched and unharmed.

Furthermore, taking all the Mount Sumeru kings from as many Buddha-lands as there are sands in the Ganges River, he places those myriad mountains within a single mountain; he then places that mountain inside a mustard seed, yet causes all the devas dwelling upon that mountain to neither perceive nor know it, nor to be disturbed by it in any way.

Furthermore, taking all sentient beings of the five destinies within as many Buddha-lands as there are sands in the Ganges River and placing them in his right palm, he then takes all the articles of pleasure from those lands and bestows them equally upon each and every sentient being without any distinction.

Furthermore, suppose all the great fires from as many Buddha-lands as there are grains of sand in the Ganges were gathered into one place at the time when the kalpa ends and they are consumed by fire; even if these fires were reduced in size to that of a single lamp wick, their fiery functions would remain exactly as before, without any difference.

Furthermore, as for all the suns and moons in as many Buddha-lands as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, if one were to emit light from a single pore to illuminate them, their brilliance would be entirely eclipsed and made to disappear.
"O Son of Heaven!
Even if I were to spend an eon, or more than an eon, describing the power of the samādhis, supernatural penetrations, and transformations of the youth Mañjuśrī, I could never reach their end."
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān transformed his own body into the form of a bhikṣu, sat to one side within the assembly, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Having now heard this description of the supernatural powers of the youth Mañjuśrī, I am unable to believe and accept it.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will manifest his spiritual power before me, so that I may behold it.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that this was an evil Māra who had transformed himself into a bhikṣu, and wishing to cause the roots of goodness in sentient beings to increase, addressed Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, saying:
"You should personally manifest the power of your supernormal abilities so that the immeasurable sentient beings in this assembly may all obtain wholesome benefit."

At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, having received the Buddha’s instruction, immediately entered the Samādhi of Sovereign Supernatural Power over the Mind of All Dharmas.
Having entered this samādhi, he exerted his supernormal powers and manifested the miraculous feats described above.
These were clearly and distinctly revealed, all appearing before him exactly as the Buddha had spoken, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Among those present at this assembly, there were none who did not see it.
At that time, the great multitude, beholding this supernatural power, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and cried out with one voice:
"Excellent, excellent!"
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, appear in the world for the sake of sentient beings;
furthermore, there are likewise Great Beings of skillful means who appear in the world and are able to manifest such inconceivable power of majestic spiritual authority.

At that time, having witnessed these various miraculous transformations, the evil Māra leaped for joy and prostrated at the feet of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. With palms joined in reverence, he addressed the Tathāgata, saying:

"The youth Mañjuśrī is truly rare and extraordinary; he is able to manifest such inconceivable supernatural transformations. Who among those who hear of this would not be struck with wonder and doubt?"

If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing this matter, are able to give rise to faith and acceptance, then even if evil Māras were as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, they would ultimately be unable to cause them harm.
“World-Honored One!
I am an evil Māra, who constantly seeks for an opportunity to harm the Buddha.
My mind delights in vexing and harming all sentient beings; if I see anyone diligently practicing the good, I will certainly use my power to create obstacles for them.”
“World-Honored One!

From this day forward, I shall deeply resolve my mind with a vow: wherever this Dharma-gate is propagated, within a hundred yojanas of any kingdom, city, town, or village, I shall remain therein like one who is blind and incapable of action, never giving rise to harm or affliction toward sentient beings.”
If one sees anyone who upholds, recites, contemplates, or explains this sutra, one must certainly give rise to respect and provide offerings and support.
World-Honored One!
My followers delight in creating obstacles for the Buddha-dharma; if they see someone practicing goodness, they will inevitably employ coercion and suppression to cause them to fall away and lose it.
"I shall now, for the sake of severing such evil deeds, proclaim a dhāraṇī.
He then spoke the mantra: "Tadyathā amale. (1)

No evil māras shall be able to find an opportunity against them; instead, it causes those māras to give rise to a joyful heart, providing offerings of clothing, bedding, food, drink, medicine, and whatever else may be required.
“World-Honored One!

If there are good men or good women who receive and uphold this mantra without ceasing day or night, they will be constantly protected by all devas, nāgas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, and no enemies or those who harbor malice shall be able to harm them.”
The Buddha said to Māra:
"Excellent, excellent!
By your reciting this dhāraṇī now, you have caused immeasurable worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to tremble in six ways."
"O Māra, you should know that this eloquence of yours is entirely produced by the supernatural power of the youth Mañjuśrī.
When the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī used his supernormal powers to cause Māra Pāpīyas to speak these mantras, thirty thousand people within the assembly all resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī had performed these transformations, he withdrew his supernormal powers and addressed the Devaputra Susampanna, saying: "Devaputra!
"I now wish to go to the Tuṣita Heaven; you should go there first and cause the assembly to gather.

When the Devaputra Suśānta heard these words, he, together with his retinue, circumambulated the Buddha and the great assembly of Bodhisattvas, including Mañjuśrī, keeping them to their right. He vanished from the midst of the gathering and, in a mere moment, arrived at that celestial palace.
Having arrived at the celestial palace, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"You all should know that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, out of compassion for us, desires to come here."
"All of you devas should abandon your heedless pleasures and assemble together for the purpose of hearing the Dharma.

When the Devaputra Suvikrānta had spoken these words, he established a *bodhimaṇḍa* within the celestial palace; that site was vast, pure, and magnificent, fashioned from various divine wish-fulfilling jewels, measuring thirty-two thousand *yojanas* from east to west and sixteen thousand *yojanas* from south to north.

Furthermore, within that space were placed immeasurable hundreds of thousands of lion thrones; these thrones were high and wide, adorned with various ornaments, and covered with celestial precious garments.
Then, having prepared the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and the lion throne (*siṃhāsana*), the Devaputra Suvikrānta bowed with palms joined and spoke thus from afar to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva:
"I have completed the tasks for which I came to the celestial palace."
"May the Benevolent One deign to descend; now is precisely the right time.

At that moment, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, together with twelve thousand bodhisattvas, fifteen hundred great śrāvakas, and countless hundreds of thousands of others—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and so forth—rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and then vanished before the Tathāgata, no longer appearing.
In a mere moment, they arrived at Tuṣita Heaven and proceeded to the site of enlightenment, where each sat upon their assigned seat as it had been prepared.

At that time, the devas of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven, and the various Brahmā assemblies of the Form Realm, announced one to another, saying:

"Now the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī is in Tuṣita Heaven about to expound the Great Dharma. We should all go together to his presence in order to hear the Dharma never heard before, and to behold various rare and marvelous things."

After these words were spoken, immeasurable and incalculable multitudes of devaputras from the realms of desire and form, in a mere instant, each departed from their respective abodes and gathered together at the Tuṣita Heaven palace.
By the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, his entire bodhimanda was fully accommodated without any crowding or constraint.
At that time, the Devaputra Suśānti addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"O Mahāsattva!..."
"Now this great assembly has all gathered; I pray that you will clarify the teachings of the Dharma through your eloquence.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the multitude, saying:
"O virtuous ones!..."
If bodhisattvas abide in four kinds of practices, they will be able to accomplish all wholesome dharmas. What are these four?
First, maintaining the precepts; second, cultivating meditative concentration; third, supernormal powers; and fourth, subduing [the mind].

If one can maintain the precepts, one will achieve extensive learning; if one can cultivate dhyāna, one will achieve prajñā; if one attains supernormal powers, one will achieve superior wisdom; and if one dwells in self-mastery, one can achieve a mind free from negligence.
Therefore, I say that if bodhisattvas abide in these four practices, they will be able to accomplish all wholesome dharmas.
"Virtuous ones!
You should know that the precepts are purified by being endowed with eight qualities."
What are these eight? First, physical conduct is upright;

second, all karmic actions are pure; third, the mind is free from blemish or defilement; fourth, one's resolve is firm and steadfast; fifth, one sustains oneself through right livelihood; sixth, one practices *dhūta* austerities with contentment; seventh, one is free from all signs of fraudulence and unreality; eighth, one never forgets the bodhicitta.
These are called the eight kinds of purity in upholding the precepts.
"Furthermore, worthy sirs!
You should know that extensive learning is also purified by eight factors.
What are these eight?

First, revering and following one's teachers and elders; second, subduing arrogance; third, diligent application and retention; fourth, correct mindfulness without error; fifth, explaining and interpreting without weariness; sixth, not being self-conceited or boastful; seventh, investigating according to principle; eighth, practicing in accordance with the teachings.
These are called the eight kinds of purity of extensive learning (*bahuśruta*).
"Furthermore, sirs! You should know that meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is also purified by eight factors.
What are these eight?

First, to constantly dwell in an araṇya, abiding in tranquil meditation and contemplation; second, not to join with crowds of people for social conversation; third, to have no greedy attachment to external objects; fourth, whether in body or mind, to renounce all worldly glory and excellence; fifth, to have few desires regarding food and drink; sixth, to be free from the state of攀緣 (pān-yuán—clinging to conditions); seventh, not to delight in refining one's voice or literary expressions; eighth, to teach others so that they may attain the bliss of the noble ones.
"Furthermore, noble sirs!
You should know that prajñā is also purified by means of eight dharmas.
What are these eight?

First, skillfully knowing the aggregates; second, skillfully knowing the elements; third, skillfully knowing the sense bases; fourth, skillfully knowing the faculties; fifth, skillfully knowing the three gates of liberation; sixth, forever uprooting the source of all afflictions; seventh, forever emerging from all hindrances, entanglements, and delusions;
eighth, forever departing from the sphere of all views. These are called the eight kinds of purity of *prajñā*.
"Furthermore, worthy sirs!
You should know that supernormal powers (abhijñā) are also purified by means of eight dharmas.
What are these eight?

First, seeing all forms without obstruction; second, hearing all sounds without limitation or partition; third, universally knowing the mental activities of sentient beings; fourth, recollecting the past without hindrance or attachment; fifth, traveling by supernormal power through all Buddha-lands; sixth, exhausting all outflows without failing at the improper time; seventh, extensively gathering roots of goodness while remaining free from all distraction and agitation;
eighth, as originally vowed, constantly acting as a virtuous friend to extensively deliver sentient beings. These are called the eight kinds of purity of supernormal powers.
"Furthermore, worthy sirs!
You should know that wisdom is also purified by eight factors.
What are these eight?

First is the knowledge of suffering, which thoroughly understands the five aggregates; second is the knowledge of origin, which forever severs all craving; third is the knowledge of cessation, which contemplates that all dependent origination is ultimately non-arising; fourth is the knowledge of the path, which is able to realize conditioned and unconditioned merits; fifth is the knowledge of cause and effect, which knows that karma and its results are not contradictory; sixth is the knowledge of certainty, which realizes the absence of self, sentient beings, and so forth; seventh is the knowledge of the three periods of time, which is skillfully able to discern the cycle of transmigration through the three times;
eighth is the knowledge of all-knowledge, which refers to the *prajñāpāramitā* that penetrates all places without exception. These are called the eight kinds of purity of knowledge.
"Furthermore, worthy sirs!
You should know that self-discipline is also purified by means of eight dharmas.
What are these eight?

First, constant inner tranquility; second, protecting one’s external conduct; third, not abandoning the triple world; fourth, conforming to dependent origination; fifth, observing that the nature of all phenomena is non-arising; sixth, observing that all phenomena have no creator; seventh, observing that all phenomena are originally without self;
eighth, ultimately not giving rise to any afflictions. These are called the eight kinds of purity of subduing.
"Furthermore, noble sirs!
You should know that heedfulness (*apramāda*) is also purified by eight dharmas.
What are these eight?

First, not defiling ethical discipline (*śīla*); second, constantly purifying extensive learning; third, accomplishing all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*); fourth, practicing wisdom (*prajñā*); fifth, being fully endowed with supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); sixth, not being conceited; seventh, extinguishing all disputes and arguments;
eighth, not regressing from wholesome dharmas. These are called the eight kinds of purity of non-heedlessness (*apramāda*).
“O virtuous ones!
If bodhisattvas abide in heedfulness, they do not lose three kinds of happiness.
What are these three?
These are the pleasures of the devas, the pleasure of meditative concentration, and the pleasure of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, one is liberated from the three evil realms.
What are these three?
These are the realm of hell-beings, the realm of animals, and the realm of hungry ghosts.
Furthermore, one is not oppressed by the three kinds of suffering.
What are these three?
That is to say: the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, and the suffering of death.
Furthermore, one is forever free from three kinds of fear. What are these three?
These are the fear of lacking a livelihood, the fear of ill repute, and the fear of the majesty and power of the great assembly.
Furthermore, one transcends the three kinds of existence (*bhava*). What are these three?
These are the existence of desire, the existence of form, and the existence of formlessness.
Furthermore, one washes away three kinds of defilements.
What are these three?
These are the stain of greed, the stain of hatred, and the stain of delusion.
Furthermore, one then fulfills the three trainings. What are these three?
These are the training in ethical discipline, the training in the mind, and the training in wisdom.
Furthermore, one attains three kinds of purity.
What are these three?
That is to say: purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind.
Furthermore, one is endowed with the three kinds of merit that are accomplished.
What are these three?
These are the merit consisting of generosity, the merit consisting of ethical discipline, and the merit consisting of cultivation.
Furthermore, one is able to cultivate the three gateways to liberation. What are these three?
These are the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Furthermore, they ensure that the three types of spiritual lineages are never severed.
What are these three?
They are the lineage of the Buddha, the lineage of the Dharma, and the lineage of the Sangha.
O virtuous ones!
The practice of heedfulness possesses such power; therefore, you all should cultivate it together.
Furthermore, O virtuous ones!
Each of the six pāramitās practiced by a bodhisattva has three specific obstacles to be overcome, which can be swiftly eliminated and severed by abiding in heedfulness.
What are these three? They are:
not practicing giving oneself while neither desiring others to give nor feeling anger toward those who are able to give;
not upholding the precepts oneself while neither desiring others to uphold them nor feeling anger toward those who are able to uphold them; [and so forth].
One who is not patient oneself yet does not wish others to be patient, and who feels anger toward those who are able to be patient;
one who is not diligent oneself yet does not wish others to be diligent, and who feels anger toward those who are able to be diligent;
one who does not cultivate meditative concentration oneself yet does not wish others to cultivate it, and who feels anger toward those who are able to cultivate it.

Being devoid of wisdom oneself and desiring that others not possess it, while resenting those who do possess it—these are called the obstacles to each of the six perfections of a bodhisattva; they are eliminated through the practice of heedfulness.
"Furthermore, noble sirs!
The six pāramitās practiced by bodhisattvas are each brought to fulfillment through three dharmas.
These three all arise from non-negligence."
What are the three?
Regarding the three aspects of giving: they are the ability to relinquish everything, not seeking karmic rewards, and dedicating the merit toward enlightenment.

Regarding the three aspects of upholding the precepts: they are receiving and bestowing with a heart of profound respect, maintaining them without deficiency, and dedicating the merit toward enlightenment.
The three aspects of patience are: gentleness and forgiveness, protecting oneself and others, and dedicating [the merit] toward enlightenment;
the three aspects of diligence are: not abandoning the yoke of virtue, being free from thoughts of coming and going, and dedicating [the merit] toward enlightenment;
the three aspects of meditative concentration are: entering all meditative absorptions, having no object of attachment, and dedicating [the merit] toward enlightenment.
The three aspects of *prajñā* are: the penetration of the light of wisdom, the cessation of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and the dedication toward enlightenment (*bodhi*).
These are called the six perfections of a bodhisattva; each of these three types is a dharma that brings about fulfillment, and they are produced through the practice of heedfulness (*apramāda*).
"Furthermore, noble sirs!
Because all bodhisattvas are heedful, they swiftly accomplish all wholesome dharmas, such as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and realize the unsurpassed enlightenment of all Buddhas."
How does one swiftly accomplish the factors conducive to enlightenment?
It is because all bodhisattvas, through non-negligence, cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness and attain their full perfection without undergoing hardship or toil.
How is it cultivated?
It means contemplating that the sphere of the body is non-existent;
contemplating that the sphere of sensation is non-existent.
One contemplates that the sphere of mind is non-existent;
one contemplates that the sphere of phenomena is non-existent.
Since nothing is apprehended in any phenomenon whatsoever, this is called the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness.
Furthermore, because they are heedful, bodhisattvas cultivate the four right endeavors and swiftly attain their fulfillment.
How do they practice them?

It is said that although bodhisattvas constantly observe that all phenomena are fundamentally unborn, unobtainable, unarisen, and without an agent—being like space—they nevertheless collect the mind and dwell correctly, applying diligent effort so that unarisen evil and unwholesome states do not arise.

Although they contemplate all phenomena as being without karma and without fruit, they collect their minds, dwell in right presence, and practice with diligence in order to cause the various evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen in sentient beings to be severed;

although they have faith and understanding that all phenomena are empty and non-existent, they collect their minds, dwell in right presence, and practice with diligence in order to cause the various wholesome states that have not yet arisen to arise;

although they know that all phenomena are originally quiescent, they collect their minds, dwell in right presence, and practice with diligence in order to cause the various wholesome states that have already arisen to remain, not to be lost, and to further increase.
Although these bodhisattvas constantly observe all phenomena, there is nothing that is done and no agent who does; their essence and characteristics are equal.

Within this, not even the slightest phenomenon can be apprehended, whether arising or ceasing, yet they always cultivate with diligence without abandoning it—this is what is called practicing right effort.
Furthermore, because they are heedful, bodhisattvas cultivate the four bases of miraculous power and swiftly attain their perfection.
How do they practice them?

It means that although bodhisattvas have forever severed desire and greed, they never abandon the aspiration for wholesome dharmas; whether by body or mind, they constantly cultivate virtuous conduct.
Although one contemplates that all phenomena are empty and unattainable, one diligently practices vigor for the sake of transforming sentient beings;
although one understands that the mind and consciousness are like illusions and transformations, one never abandons the aspiration to perfect awakening and fulfill all Buddha-dharmas;

although one knows that all phenomena are without support or activity and cannot be grasped or attached to, one constantly reflects upon what has been heard in accordance with reality—this is called the cultivation of the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Furthermore, because they are heedful, bodhisattvas cultivate the five faculties and swiftly bring them to fulfillment.
How do they cultivate them?

It is said that although these bodhisattvas attain awakening through their own power without hearing it from others, they nevertheless teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to understand and give rise to deep faith.
Although they have no thought of coming and no thought of going, they diligently and universally practice all deeds of omniscience;
although they have neither recollection nor memory regarding objective realms, they remain neither forgetful nor deluded therein;
although they clearly comprehend all phenomena through the light of wisdom, they are always in right concentration, tranquil and unmoving.
Although they constantly abide in the equal nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they sever all veils, obscurations, conceptual proliferations, and discriminations.
This is called the cultivation of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).
Furthermore, because these bodhisattvas are heedful, they cultivate the five powers (*pañcabala*) and swiftly attain their fulfillment.
How is this practiced?
It means that when bodhisattvas cultivate the power of faith, no external treatises can shake them;
when they cultivate the power of diligence, no evil māras can obstruct or destroy them.
By cultivating the power of mindfulness, one does not enter the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
by cultivating the power of meditative concentration, one swiftly attains detachment from the afflictions of the five hindrances;
and by the power of wisdom, one never again grasps at the objective realms of various views.
This is called the cultivation of the five powers.
Furthermore, because they are heedful, bodhisattvas cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment and swiftly attain their perfection.
How do they cultivate them?
That is to say, when Bodhisattvas never forget or lose any wholesome dharmas, this is the cultivation of the awakening factor of mindfulness;
when they constantly delight in observing dependent origination, this is the cultivation of the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena;
and when they practice the path to enlightenment without ever regressing, this is the cultivation of the awakening factor of vigor.
To know the Dharma and be content, without any further longing, is the cultivation of the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*);
to distance oneself from the faults of physical and mental agitation is the cultivation of the awakening factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*);
and to enter the liberations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness is the cultivation of the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
To be free from the mind that seeks further learning regarding arising is the cultivation of the awakening factor of equanimity.
This is called the cultivation of the dharma of the seven factors of awakening.
Furthermore, by means of heedfulness, all bodhisattvas cultivate the eightfold noble path and swiftly attain its perfection.
How is it cultivated?
It is called the cultivation of right view because of being forever free from the views of annihilationism and eternalism;
it is called the cultivation of right intention because of being free from thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harmfulness.
Because it is free from inequality between self and others, it is called the cultivation of right speech;
because it is free from the characteristics of flattery, hypocrisy, and unreality, it is called the cultivation of right livelihood;
because it is free from the affairs of a timid body and mind, it is called the cultivation of right action.
Because one is free from the conceit of self-satisfaction and the mind that looks down upon others, it is called the cultivation of right effort;
because one is free from all dullness and delusion, it is called the cultivation of right mindfulness;
and because one stills all discursive conceptualization, it is called the cultivation of right concentration.
This is called the cultivation of the eightfold noble path.
O virtuous ones!

By the meaning previously explained, I say that when Bodhisattvas abide in heedfulness, they will achieve all wholesome dharmas, such as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and realize the unsurpassed enlightenment of all Buddhas.
"O virtuous ones!
This heedful bodhisattva, having entered into such factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), emerges from the mire of all birth and death."
Having emerged from birth and death, one perceives nothing at all in any phenomena.
Because there is nothing perceived, there is nothing to be expressed.
Because there is nothing to be expressed, one enters ultimate tranquility.
What is meant by "ultimate tranquility"?

Because all phenomena are uncreated, and because they are uncreated they cannot be grasped; because they cannot be grasped they have no utility; because they have no utility they cannot be established as existing; and because they cannot be established as existing, one should know that this is ultimate tranquility.
When this Dharma was being taught, twelve thousand devaputras in the assembly were freed from dust and removed from defilement, and their Dharma-eye became pure.
At that time, the devaputra Suśānti again addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
“O Mahāsattva!
"What is called 'practicing the bodhisattva path'?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva replied, "O Devaputra! "
If a bodhisattva, though not abandoning birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), is not defiled by the evils of birth-and-death;
though not dwelling in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), constantly cultivates the merit of the unconditioned;
and though fully practicing the six *pāramitās*, manifests the conduct of *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.
This is called practicing the bodhisattva path.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra,
although a bodhisattva is pure within emptiness, they skillfully manifest all objective realms, yet do not grasp at those realms."
Although they are purified within the signless, they skillfully enter into all signs, yet they do not cling to signs.
Although they are purified within the wishless, they skillfully traverse the three realms, yet they do not become attached to the realms.
Although he dwells in the purity of non-arising and non-ceasing, he skillfully explains arising and ceasing, yet he does not undergo arising or ceasing. Why is this?

This Bodhisattva who has tamed his mind, while thoroughly understanding that all phenomena are empty and non-existent, perceives that sentient beings give rise to views and attachments within their sensory realms; because of these views and attachments, their afflictions increase.
The Bodhisattva, wishing to cause them to sever all attachments to views, expounds the Dharma for them, causing them to know that all objective realms are empty.
As it is taught regarding emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, so it is likewise with non-arising and non-ceasing.
This is called practicing the bodhisattva path.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra,
that which involves going forth and returning is called practicing the bodhisattva path."
What is meant by "going forth" and "returning"?
To observe the inclinations and desires of all sentient beings is called "going forth";
to preach the Dharma to them according to what is appropriate for each is called "returning."
To enter samādhi oneself is called "going";
to cause all sentient beings to attain samādhi is called "returning.
To practice the noble path oneself is called "going";
To be able to teach and transform all ordinary beings is called "returning.
To personally attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is called "going";
to cause all sentient beings to likewise attain this patience is called "returning."
To personally emerge from birth and death through skillful means is called "going";
to cause sentient beings to likewise attain liberation is called "returning.
To delight in mental tranquility is called "going";
To constantly remain within birth and death to teach and transform sentient beings is called "returning.
To diligently observe one's own practice of going and returning is called "going";
to preach such a Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings is called "returning."
Cultivating the liberations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness is called "going";
preaching the Dharma for the sake of causing sentient beings to sever the three types of discursive thought and mental observation is called "returning."
Firmly making a vow is called "going";
rescuing and delivering sentient beings in accordance with that vow is called "returning.
Vowing to give rise to the bodhicitta and sit at the site of enlightenment is called "going."
To fully cultivate the practices performed by Bodhisattvas is called "returning.
This is what is meant by the Bodhisattva’s path of going and returning.
When this Dharma was being taught, five hundred Bodhisattvas within the assembly all attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
At that time, the Devaputra Suśānti addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"O Mahāsattva!
I have heard of a world called Sarvaguṇaprabhāsa. In which direction does such a world lie?"
"What is the name of the Buddha who preaches the Dharma therein?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva replied,
"O Son of Heaven, above this world, passing through Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of twelve Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Sarvaguṇaprabhāsa."
"The Buddha there is named Samantabhadra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who expounds the True Dharma within this land.
The Devaputra Suvikrānta said,
"O Mahāsattva!"
"My heart desires to see that world and that Tathāgata; I only pray that you, out of your benevolence, will show me so that I may behold them.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva immediately entered samādhi.

This samādhi is named "Stainless Radiance. From within his body, he emits various kinds of light; these rays of light ascend, penetrating twelve Ganges-sands of Buddha-lands, reaching the world-system called "Radiance of All Merits," where various colored lights fill that land entirely.
When those bodhisattvas saw this light, they attained what they had never experienced before; with palms joined in reverence, they addressed the Tathāgata Samantabhadra, saying:
"World-Honored One!
From where does this radiance come?"
The Buddha Samantabhadra said: "Good son!

Below here, past as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in twelve Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Sahā. The Buddha there is named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; he currently dwells there, expounding the teachings of the Dharma."

There is a bodhisattva there named Mañjuśrī, who dwells in the stage of non-retrogression and has entered the Samādhi of Stainless Radiance. From within his body he emits various kinds of light, and these rays extend far to immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds in the ten directions, completely filling each and every world; for this reason, there is this radiance now.
Those bodhisattvas further spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
We now all wish to behold Śākyamuni Buddha of the Sahā world, as well as the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.”

At that time, the Tathāgata Samantabhadra emitted a great radiance from within the thousand-spoked wheel mark on the sole of his foot. That light shone brilliantly, passing through Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of twelve Ganges Rivers in the direction below, and its brilliance pervaded this entire world-system.
By means of the Buddha’s radiance, those bodhisattvas were all able to see this Sahā world, as well as Śākyamuni Buddha and the assembly of bodhisattvas;
likewise, the bodhisattvas of this land also saw that country, along with Samantabhadra Tathāgata and the multitude of his bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Tathāgata Samantabhadra addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"In the Sahā world, the Great Dharma is constantly being preached. Among you, who is able to go there to listen and receive it?"
In the assembly, there was a bodhisattva named Jñānolkadhara who rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, I now wish, by relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power, to go to the Sahā world; I only pray that the Tathāgata will look upon me with compassion and grant me permission.”
The Tathāgata Samantabhadra said: "Good son!
Now is precisely the time; you should go there with haste."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānolkadhara, together with ten billion other bodhisattvas, bowed his head in reverent salutation to the Tathāgata Samantabhadra, joined his palms in respect, and circumambulated him seven times to the right.

Passing away from that land, in the time it takes a strong man to flex and extend his arm, he arrived before the assembly of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva in the Well-Situated Pavilion of the Tuṣita Heaven Palace in the Sahā world.
Bowing with palms joined, he paid homage at the feet of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and spoke these words:
"O Great Being!

The light you have extended has reached our land. Our World-Honored One, Samantabhadra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, has granted us permission to come to this world in order to see the Great Being, pay him honor, gaze upon him, and hear the Dharma."
At that time, when the devaputras of the desire and form realms saw the bodhisattvas who had come from those lands, they all spoke these words:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Inconceivable! Most rare, most rare indeed!

Mañjuśrī, the Great Being of skillful means, possesses such supernatural transformations that, by the power of samādhi, he emits this radiance and is able to reach those worlds in the zenith, causing all the bodhisattvas there to come swiftly."

At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva further proclaimed the sublime Dharma extensively for the great assembly. Among the multitude, seventy-two nayutas of devaputras gave rise to profound faith and understanding, and resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, having completed his tasks in the Tuṣita Heaven palace, vanished from the celestial palace without rising from his seat, together with the various bodhisattvas, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and immeasurable devas, as well as all the bodhisattvas who had come from the land of Universal Radiance of All Merits.

In a single thought-moment, they arrived at the presence of the Buddha; all rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and with palms joined in reverence, circumambulated him seven times to the right.
Having finished circumambulating the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Grasping the Torch of Wisdom, together with ten billion of his peers, came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Samantabhadra Tathāgata sends his greetings and asks after your well-being: Are you free from illness and affliction, and do you dwell in peace and happiness?

At that time, the World-Honored One, having comforted the bodhisattvas according to the Dharma, surveyed the entire assembly that had gathered and commanded them to be seated again. He then extensively expounded the Dharma for them, and there was none who did not rejoice.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the assembly, saying:

"You should know that this youth Mañjuśrī and the Bodhisattva Jñānolkadhara have manifested these miraculous transformations out of a desire to bring immeasurable sentient beings to spiritual maturity."
These two great beings have already accomplished various skillful means and attained wisdom and eloquence regarding profound principles.
Having performed Buddha-work for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, they have been born into this world for the sake of sentient beings.

If there are sentient beings who manage to see these two bodhisattvas, you should know that they will attain mastery over their six sense faculties and shall never again enter the realm of the various māras.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānolkadhara and the assembly of bodhisattvas who had come with him entered this land and beheld the World-Honored One.
By hearing the Dharma, they realized the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Having attained patience, they circumambulated the Buddha to the right and paid homage at his feet.
At that moment, this trichiliocosm shook; these bodhisattvas then vanished before the Buddha and, in an instant, returned to their own lands.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Elder Ānanda, saying:
“You should uphold this Dharma-gate and expound it widely for others.
Ānanda said:
"Yes, World-Honored One!
What should this Dharma-gate be named?"
"How should it be upheld?
The Buddha said, "This Dharma-gate is named 'The Inconceivable Realm of the Buddhas Spoken by Mañjuśrī'; uphold it thus."

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Devaputra Suśreṣṭha, the Elder Ānanda, and all those in the world—gods, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others—were filled with great joy, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.
The Sūtra on the Inconceivable Realm of the Buddhas Spoken by Mañjuśrī, Scroll II.
